prompt.context: Our client owns a large hotel chain and is thinking about investing in an add-on waterpark on one of its properties. This has been tested in some places and has a lot of potential benefits: family friendly, year-round availability, and potential to bring in new clientele. They have done a lot of work surveying their chain and believe that they have found the right hotel to experiment with a waterpark add-on. Currently, this hotel has a lot of business travelers, but our client believes it would also be attractive for families. Our client is nervous about the capital required to build the add-on and wants to make sure that they are making the right investment.
prompt.question: Should our client make the waterpark investment? Specifically, how much will the hotel need to charge per room to recoup its costs?

clarifying_info.q: Are there any competitors with nearby waterparks?
clarifying_info.a: There are no competitors immediately nearby for a waterpark. There is no possibility for a competitive response in the short run.

clarifying_info.q: What does the market research show about demand?
clarifying_info.a: Our client has done proper diligence and has determined this is the right location. We do not have any specifics about the market and are unable to conduct additional survey data.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the current hotel guests?
clarifying_info.a: The hotel's normal clientele is business travelers, but the waterpark is expected to also bring in families.
$6 million investment with a 3-year payback target.

clarifying_info.q: How many rooms does the hotel have?
What occupancy rate should we assume?
clarifying_info.a: With the waterpark, assume 50% vacancy on average for the year.
Variable cost is $40 per night per room. The $6 million investment is a fixed cost.

clarifying_info.q: How many days per year should we use?

framework: 1. Cost structure — identify fixed costs (the $6M investment) and variable costs ($40/room/night), and establish the 3-year payback period
2. Breakeven analysis — calculate the minimum nightly room charge needed to recover the fixed investment over 3 years, then add variable cost for total required rate
3. Pricing interpretation — assess whether the resulting breakeven price is high or low relative to real hotel rates and what premium can be charged
4. Additional revenue streams — identify other ways the waterpark generates income beyond room rates
5. Risks and issues — qualitative assessment of operational, regulatory, competitive, and customer-mix risks

questions.prompt: How much will the hotel need to charge per room per night to recoup its investment in 3 years?
questions.guidance: Candidate should spread the fixed $6M investment over 3 years to get annual revenue needed, then divide by annual room-nights (rooms × occupancy rate × days/year). Add variable cost to get total required rate. Strong candidates recognise 350 days (not 365), use 50% occupancy correctly, and arrive cleanly at ~$30 fixed cost + $40 variable = ~$70/night total.

math.setup: Annual fixed cost recovery = $6M / 3 years. Annual room-nights = 400 rooms × 50% occupancy × 350 days. Breakeven fixed cost per room = annual fixed cost / annual room-nights. Total required rate = fixed cost per room + variable cost per room.
steps: $6,000,000 / 3 = $2,000,000 per year in fixed cost recovery needed
400 rooms × 50% occupancy = 200 occupied rooms per night
200 occupied rooms × 350 days = 70,000 room-nights per year
$2,000,000 / 70,000 = ~$28.57, round to ~$30 per night in fixed cost
math.answer: ~$70 per room per night for the 3-year payback period

questions.prompt: How should we interpret the $70/night breakeven number? What does it imply about the investment attractiveness?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognise that $70/night is extremely low for a hotel with a waterpark amenity, especially for families. Hotels targeting families can typically charge well above this. This means the hotel can charge a significant premium above breakeven, making the investment highly attractive economically. Strong candidates draw on personal knowledge of hotel pricing.

brainstorming.prompt: What other potential revenue streams and risks/issues should we consider for this waterpark investment?

categories.name: Additional revenue streams
ideas: Charging a separate admission/entry fee for waterpark access
Food and beverage restaurants inside the park
Promotional tie-ins with brands or local attractions
Expansion of the waterpark model to other hotels in the chain

categories.name: Potential risks and issues
ideas: Management competency — does the hotel chain have any experience operating theme parks or waterparks?
Regulatory and insurance risks associated with waterpark operations
Health and litigation risks (slip and fall, drowning liability)
Competitive response from other hotel chains once the concept is validated
Alienating existing business traveler clientele with a family-friendly atmosphere
Seasonality risk if year-round attendance is lower than projected
Maintenance and ongoing capital expenditure for waterpark equipment

recommendation: The client should proceed with the waterpark investment. The economics are extremely attractive: the breakeven price of ~$70/room/night is very low relative to what a hotel with waterpark amenities can realistically charge, implying a substantial margin above the required rate.
The investment pays back in 3 years and opens multiple additional revenue streams (admissions, F&B, merchandise) beyond room revenue alone.
risks: Operational inexperience — hotel chains typically lack waterpark management expertise; mitigation is to hire specialized operators or partner with an experienced waterpark operator
Liability and regulatory exposure — waterparks carry significant insurance and litigation risk that must be priced into the investment
Potential alienation of the existing business traveler base if the property atmosphere shifts too family-oriented
next_steps: Confirm realistic achievable room rates with the waterpark (market survey of comparable family resort hotels) to quantify upside above the $70 breakeven
Assess management capability and determine whether to hire specialized staff or engage an outsourced operator
Model additional revenue streams (admissions, F&B, merchandise) to build a full P&L for the investment
Pilot at this one property, measure NPS from both family and business segments, then decide on chain-wide rollout
